title: Better Together, in the Right Order: Classical-then-LLM Optimization for SE

edges.target: EZR (Ganguly & Menzies; Senthilkumar & Menzies)
edges.ref: [28] K. K. Ganguly and T. Menzies, 'How low can you go? the data-light se challenge,' in FSE'26, 2026.
edges.evidence: EZR [3], [28] is our opt3 method and the no-LLM control ... the exact configuration Ganguly et al. [28] report beating the classical state of the art ... so we adopt it unchanged.

edges.target: EZR active-learning loop (as SNAP2 warm-start substrate)
edges.ref: [28] K. K. Ganguly and T. Menzies, 'How low can you go? the data-light se challenge,' in FSE'26, 2026.
edges.evidence: SNAP 2 replaces SNAP's random warm start with the output of a short EZR run. EZR spends the first half of its labeling budget acquiring informative rows.

edges.target: OPRO (Yang et al.)
edges.ref: [21] C. Yang, X. Wang, Y. Lu, H. Liu, Q. V. Le, D. Zhou, and X. Chen, 'Large language models as optimizers,' ICLR 2024.
edges.evidence: SNAP is our extension to OPRO [21]. OPRO's main loop shows the LLM a trajectory of tried points and asks for the next.

edges.target: BS_LLM warm-start baseline (Senthilkumar & Menzies)
edges.ref: [3] L. Senthilkumar and T. Menzies, 'Can large language models improve se active learning via warm-starts?' TOSEM, 2024.
edges.evidence: SNAP 2 (85%) tops every LLM-first method by eleven points or more (BS_LLM 74%, SYNTHCORE 70%), a gap outside the cluster band of RQ1.
edges.section: III Algorithms; Table II; V RQ3

edges.target: SynthCore (Senthilkumar & Menzies)
edges.ref: [37] L. Senthilkumar and T. Menzies, 'From brittle to robust: Improving llm annotations for se optimization,' EMSE, vol. 31, no. 6, p. 155, 2026.
edges.evidence: SYNTHCORE [37] seeds by clustered ensemble prompting. DBSCAN [43] pre-clusters the labeled rows. Across M independent sessions ... the model is asked to synthesize a row better than the best seen so far.
edges.section: III Algorithms; Table II; V RQ3

edges.target: Ganguly FSE'26 benchmark result: EZR beats SMAC3, TPE, DEHB, qEHVI/MOEA-D on MOOT (not re-run)
edges.ref: [28] K. K. Ganguly and T. Menzies, 'How low can you go? the data-light se challenge,' in FSE'26, 2026.

edges.target: Cliff's delta
edges.ref: [49] N. Cliff, 'Dominance statistics: Ordinal analyses to answer ordinal questions,' Psychological Bulletin, vol. 114, no. 3, 1993.
edges.evidence: Cliff's delta [49], |delta| = |#(x>y) - #(x<y)| / (nm), is below 0.195 (small [50])

edges.target: Cliff's delta 'small' threshold 0.195 (Hess & Kromrey)
edges.ref: [50] M. R. Hess and J. D. Kromrey, 'Robust confidence intervals for effect sizes: A comparative study of Cohen's d and Cliff's delta ...,' AERA, 2004.
edges.evidence: is below 0.195 (small [50])

edges.target: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (Massey)
edges.ref: [51] F. J. Massey, 'The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for goodness of fit,' JASA, vol. 46, no. 253, pp. 68-78, 1951.
edges.evidence: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic [51] (max distance between the empirical cumulative distributions) is below 1.36 sqrt((n+m)/(nm)) (95% confidence).

edges.target: Cohen 0.2-sigma indistinguishability rule (Sawilowsky)
edges.ref: [53] S. S. Sawilowsky, 'New effect size rules of thumb,' Journal of Modern Applied Statistical Methods, vol. 8, no. 2, p. 26, 2009.
edges.evidence: Cohen comments that events are indistinguishably different if they differ by less than .2 sigma [53]. For a Gaussian of range -3 sigma to +3 sigma, this 0.2 is a target of size p

edges.target: Probable correctness theory (Hamlet)
edges.ref: [52] R. G. Hamlet, 'Probable correctness theory,' Information Processing Letters, vol. 25, no. 1, pp. 17-25, 1987.
edges.evidence: Hamlet [52] comments on the number of samples B required to be C confident of finding a target with probability p is C = 1 - (1-p)^B

edges.target: B<=20 labeling-budget argument (Ganguly & Menzies)
edges.ref: [28] K. K. Ganguly and T. Menzies, 'How low can you go? the data-light se challenge,' in FSE'26, 2026.
edges.evidence: Table III offers a mathematical argument from Ganguly et al. [28] that, with sufficient knowledge (e.g. from an LLM), it is possible to find good solutions with B <= 20.

edges.target: Cohen's advice to compare against simple baselines
edges.ref: [41] P. R. Cohen, Empirical methods for artificial intelligence. MIT Press, 1995.
edges.evidence: Cohen advises checking complex methods against simple ones [41], so we add two no-LLM floors: RANDOM and the 2018 search-based method RRP [42].

edges.target: 'Reference optimal' concept (Cohen; McGeoch)
edges.ref: [54] C. C. McGeoch, A guide to experimental algorithmics. Cambridge University Press, 2012.
edges.evidence: Here 'optimal' means reference optimal, a term from the empirical-algorithms literature [41], [54]: the best solution observed so far.

edges.target: Pareto-based SBSE evaluation review (Li, Chen, Yao) -- HV/Chebyshev cross-check
edges.ref: [47] M. Li, T. Chen, and X. Yao, 'How to evaluate solutions in pareto-based search-based software engineering: A critical review and methodological guidance,' IEEE TSE, vol. 48, no. 5, 2022.
edges.evidence: A recent IEEE TSE article by Chen et al. [47] reviewed various multi-objective optimization performance measures like hypervolume ... we also computed both metrics; the ranking is consistent

edges.target: Argument that HV/spread/GD/IGD are misguided for SE (Chen; Ganguly)
edges.ref: [2] P. Chen and T. Chen, 'Promisetune ...,' ICSE 2026; [28] K. K. Ganguly and T. Menzies, 'How low can you go?,' FSE'26.
edges.evidence: Subsequent work by Chen [2], as well as analogous research by Ganguly [28] suggests that these measures are somewhat misguided ... Hence, here, we used d2h rather than HV, spread, GD and IGD.

edges.target: Huang et al. finding that standalone LLMs match conventional heuristics on continuous benchmarks
edges.ref: [27] B. Huang, X. Wu, Y. Zhou, J. Wu, L. Feng, R. Cheng, and K. C. Tan, 'Exploring the true potential: Evaluating the black-box optimization capability of LLMs,' arXiv:2404.06290, 2024.
edges.evidence: OPRO was validated only on continuous benchmarks ... where Huang et al. found standalone LLMs no better than conventional heuristics [27]. MOOT data is largely symbolic, so we adapt OPRO

edges.target: Prior pessimistic verdicts on LLM optimizers: useful only on small problems [3], only as subroutine [24], too slow [28]
edges.ref: [3] L. Senthilkumar and T. Menzies, TOSEM 2024; [24] A. Schwanke et al., 'Multiobjective hierarchical optimization with large language models,' arXiv:2601.13892, 2026; [28] K. K. Ganguly and T. Menzies, FSE'26.
edges.evidence: Reports range from limited advantage over conventional heuristics [27], to useful only on small problems [3], to useful only as a search subroutine [24], to too slow to be practical [28].

edges.target: EZR re-run unchanged in Ganguly's FSE'26 configuration on the same MOOT corpus
edges.ref: [28] K. K. Ganguly and T. Menzies, 'How low can you go? the data-light se challenge,' in FSE'26, 2026.
edges.evidence: EZR (71%) is the strongest no-LLM method and our classical anchor (and recall that Ganguly et al. showed EZR also beats many classical methods such as TPE, SMAC3, and DEHB on these same tasks [28]).

edges.target: LLM warm-start methods (BS_LLM, SynthCore) re-evaluated at scale across 105 MOOT tasks
edges.ref: [3] L. Senthilkumar and T. Menzies, TOSEM 2024; [37] L. Senthilkumar and T. Menzies, EMSE 2026.
edges.evidence: Studies here often report five datasets or fewer [3] ... The LLM-bearing methods SNAP (75%) and BS_LLM (74%) sit just above EZR, and SYNTHCORE (70%) very nearly ties with it.

edges.target: Active learning definition (Settles)
edges.ref: [40] B. Settles, Active learning. Morgan & Claypool Publishers, 2012.
edges.evidence: It can be surprisingly small when SMO uses active learning [40]. A passive learner builds its model from all the data. An active learner instead reflects on the model built so far

edges.target: Over 40% of MySQL/Apache/Hadoop failures trace to configuration errors (Yin et al.)

edges.evidence: over 40% of failures trace to configuration errors [12], as do most cloud production outages [13].
